sentences.text: This ancient fish possessed a snout that extended for half of its entire body length.
Its body carried two dorsal fins, three anal fins, and a long, tapering tail fin known as heterocercal.
The original specimen was a young individual trapped inside a hard rock formation in Illinois.
Scientists found preserved remains of jointed arthropods inside the fish's digestive tract.
The genus was formally introduced to science in 1969 by the paleontologist Rainer Zangerl.
The name honors Ray Bandringa, the person who originally located the fossil.
Researchers believe it hunted in cloudy water using suction feeding and needle-like spines along its cheeks.
Since every known individual from the Mazon Creek site is young, the location might have acted as a nursery.
Its life cycle appears to be the reverse of salmon, with adults residing in fresh water and juveniles in saltier environments.
This genus is monotypic, containing only the single species B. rayi within the family Bandringidae.
It belongs to the class Chondrichthyes, which includes cartilaginous fish.
The animal lived during the Pennsylvanian subperiod of the Carboniferous period.
Specifically, it existed between 315.2 and 307 million years ago during the Moscovian age.
Its exact relationship to other elasmobranchs remains uncertain, although it was once considered an unusual member of the order Ctenacanthiformes.
